summary: Points out gaps in the official Host-Host protocol found while building the network software. Cases such as error control messages, unusual message types, and messages flagged as coming from the IMP were not clearly described. The note suggests how implementations should handle these edge cases.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 117 records protocol gaps found while implementing NCP software. It suggests details for error reports and a RESET exchange to clear stale connection state after a site failure.

questions: what gaps were found in the host-host protocol
how should an ncp handle unexpected messages
what gaps did implementers find in the ncp protocol

what is a reset mechanism in networking
subtitle: Implementation comments on errors and unusual messages in the Host-Host protocol.

tldr.problem: NCP implementers found that the official protocol did not clearly explain ERR commands, several IMP message types and messages with the From-IMP bit set.
tldr.mechanism: J. Wong lists error cases and suggests what information ERR commands should include, plus a RESET and RESET-reply exchange for recovering site state.
tldr.outcome: The note offers implementation suggestions and identifies From-IMP messages as an area needing classification.

today: The unit metadata records RFC 117 as Unknown and lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text is implementation commentary on the official protocol, dated 7 April 1971.

sections.title: ERR Commands and Error Details
sections.content:
The note lists errors such as illegal operation codes, incomplete commands, invalid socket polarity, requests on nonexistent links and sending more data than allocated. It also adds cases involving connections that exist but are not established, and control commands with the wrong number of data bits.

Wong proposes an 8-bit error code, an 80-bit field for the command in error, and additional fields for socket numbers or other context. The extra information varies by error so an implementer can identify what failed.
sections.plainLanguage: An error report should identify the type of error and include the failed command. It may also need link numbers, socket numbers or other details to explain the problem.

sections.title: IMP Messages and Site Failures
sections.content:
The RFC identifies IMP-to-host message types 2, 7 and 9 as cases that can cause implementation difficulty. Type 7 or 9 can indicate that a destination host or IMP is unavailable or that transmission is incomplete.

If a remote host goes down after connections were established, local NCP tables may retain misleading entries. The proposed recovery is for a starting NCP to send RESET to every other site; a RESET-reply sets that site's up-bit, and messages are sent only to sites whose up-bit is set. A received RESET clears that site's table entries and receives an immediate reply.
sections.plainLanguage: When a remote site fails, old connection entries can become misleading. The proposal uses RESET and RESET-reply messages to clear those entries and mark a site ready again.

sections.title: Messages Marked as From the IMP
sections.content:
The note says messages with the From-IMP bit set are not discussed in the protocol material. It reports that some statistical measurements had been made and says the messages should be classified.

Wong also says the proposed RESET exchange would make ECO and ERP commands unnecessary and recommends removing them.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC does not explain what all From-IMP messages represent and calls for classifying them. It also recommends removing ECO and ERP if RESET is introduced.
